Uzbekistan Electric Utilities Workers Walk Out, Disrupting Power Generation

TASHKENT, June 12 — Workers at several major electric utilities in Uzbekistan, including Uzbekenergo SJSC, staged a walkout on Wednesday, causing widespread disruptions in power generation and distribution across the country.

The strike, organized by the Union of Electric Utility Workers of Uzbekistan, began early in the morning and involved technicians, engineers, and support staff at power plants and distribution centers. Union leaders cited unresolved wage disputes and calls for improved working conditions as the main reasons behind the industrial action.

By midday, Uzbekenergo SJSC reported that approximately 30% of its workforce had joined the walkout, leading to reduced output at multiple thermal and hydroelectric stations. A spokesperson for the company said, “We are doing everything possible to maintain essential services, but the ongoing action has forced us to implement rolling blackouts in several regions.”

Local residents in Tashkent, Samarkand, and parts of the Ferghana Valley reported intermittent outages and reduced voltage as power grids struggled to cope with the shortages. In a statement, the Ministry of Energy acknowledged the disruptions and urged the striking workers to return to negotiations. “We understand the concerns raised by employees and remain committed to dialogue. However, the continuation of these actions threatens the stability of our national power supply,” the statement said.

Analysts warned that prolonged industrial action could have significant consequences for the country’s electric utilities sector. “This is the first coordinated walkout of this scale since the sector’s major restructuring in the early 2010s,” said Timur Abdujalilov, an energy sector analyst based in Tashkent. “If the strike continues, it could impact maintenance schedules and delay planned upgrades at several key facilities.”

The walkout has also affected operations at Central Asian Power Company, which reported temporary shutdowns at two substations. The company said backup generators were being deployed but admitted that capacity was limited.

Union representatives said they would not return to work until their demands for higher wages and safer working conditions were addressed. “Our members have been patient, but the current situation is unsustainable,” said union leader Nodira Karimova. “We hope for a swift resolution but are prepared to continue until our voices are heard.”

As negotiations continued into the evening, many communities braced for further supply disruptions. The Ministry of Energy said contingency plans were being implemented but did not specify when normal service would resume. The strike was ongoing at the time of writing.
